name: portal cavernoma
aliases: cavernous transformation of the portal vein

reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
clinicalPearls: A portal cavernoma is the network of hepatopetal collateral veins that develops around a chronically obstructed or thrombosed portal vein, a process termed cavernous transformation.
It is the hallmark of chronic extrahepatic portal vein obstruction, and in the absence of cirrhosis liver synthetic function is typically well preserved.

In children it commonly follows neonatal umbilical vein catheterisation, omphalitis or sepsis, whereas in adults prothrombotic states, myeloproliferative neoplasms, cirrhosis, abdominal sepsis and malignancy predominate.
The dominant clinical problem is portal hypertension with gastro-oesophageal varices, splenomegaly and hypersplenism.
Variceal bleeding is often surprisingly well tolerated because hepatic function is preserved.
The collaterals can compress the biliary tree to produce portal cavernoma cholangiopathy, also called portal biliopathy.
Doppler ultrasound shows the serpiginous collaterals replacing the normal portal vein, and CT or MR portography maps the anatomy for intervention.
The Meso-Rex bypass, which restores physiological portal inflow, is the preferred operation in suitable children.
reference.pathophysiology: When the main portal vein is obstructed by thrombosis, extrinsic compression or malformation, the portal circulation seeks alternative routes to reach the liver. Over weeks to months the pre-existing tiny peribiliary and paracholedochal veins in the porta hepatis dilate and proliferate into a leash of tortuous hepatopetal collaterals, the cavernoma, which partially bypasses the occluded segment. Because these collaterals cannot fully substitute for the calibre of the native vein, portal pressure rises and drives the formation of portosystemic collaterals including gastro-oesophageal varices, together with splenomegaly and hypersplenism. In extrahepatic obstruction the intrahepatic parenchyma and its arterial supply remain intact, so hepatic synthetic function is generally preserved and bleeding is better tolerated than in cirrhotic portal hypertension. The engorged periductal collaterals may in turn compress and distort the bile ducts, producing cholangiopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis or idiopathic portal hypertension
Portal vein tumour thrombus from hepatocellular carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasound of the portal system
Thrombophilia and myeloproliferative neoplasm screen including JAK2 mutation testing
Full blood count to assess hypersplenism
Liver function and synthetic tests to confirm preserved function
redFlags: Acute variceal haemorrhage with haematemesis or melaena
Extension of thrombosis into the mesenteric veins with bowel ischaemia
Rapid splenic enlargement with severe cytopenias
reference.prognosis: With preserved hepatic function the long-term outlook is generally good once varices are controlled, though recurrent bleeding, hypersplenism and biliopathy contribute to morbidity, and extension of thrombosis to the mesenteric veins is a serious threat.
pitfalls: Assuming portal hypertension implies cirrhosis and overlooking a non-cirrhotic cavernoma with preserved liver function.
Failing to screen for and treat an underlying prothrombotic or myeloproliferative disorder.
Missing associated portal biliopathy as a cause of cholestasis.
Delaying recognition of mesenteric extension causing intestinal ischaemia.
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Anticoagulation directed by the underlying prothrombotic state, balanced against variceal bleeding risk after endoscopic assessment
Prevention and treatment of gastro-oesophageal variceal bleeding with endoscopic band ligation and non-selective beta-blockade, and surveillance endoscopy
Meso-Rex bypass, restoring physiological portal flow, or a portosystemic shunt for refractory variceal bleeding or symptomatic portal hypertension, particularly in children
Management of hypersplenism and its cytopenias, with attention to bleeding risk
Treatment of coexisting portal cavernoma cholangiopathy when biliary obstruction develops
Haematology referral to identify and treat an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm or thrombophilia, with monitoring for extension of thrombosis into the mesenteric veins
